To "bury one's head in the sand" means to deliberately ignore a problem, danger, or uncomfortable truth instead of facing it. The person knows something is wrong, but they choose to look away and pretend it doesn't exist — hoping it will somehow disappear on its own.

The key word here is deliberately. This idiom is not about someone who simply doesn't know about a problem. It's about someone who knows there's a problem but refuses to acknowledge it or deal with it.

Think of it this way: imagine your roof is leaking. A person who buries their head in the sand doesn't call a repair person. They don't even talk about it. They just put a bucket under the drip, go to sleep, and tell themselves "I'm sure it'll be fine." That is the essence of this idiom.
Where It Comes From (The Origin)

This idiom comes from a very old belief about ostriches — the large, flightless birds found in Africa. For centuries, people believed that when an ostrich sensed danger approaching, it would plunge its head into the sand. The idea was that the ostrich thought: "If I can't see the danger, then the danger can't see me either."

Of course, this is completely illogical — hiding your eyes doesn't make a threat disappear. But that's exactly why the image became such a powerful metaphor for human foolishness. When we say someone is "burying their head in the sand," we are comparing them to this silly, self-deceiving ostrich.

The earliest written references to this behavior trace back to the ancient Roman writer Pliny the Elder (around 77 AD), who described ostriches hiding their heads in bushes when threatened. Over many centuries, the story got exaggerated and changed — "bushes" became "sand" — and eventually entered the English language as a full idiom.
But Wait — Do Ostriches Actually Do This?

No. This is a myth.

Real ostriches do not bury their heads in sand to escape danger. Here is what they actually do:

  • They run. Ostriches are the fastest two-legged animals on Earth, reaching speeds of up to 70 km/h (about 45 mph). Running away is their primary defense.
  • They lie flat. When they can't run, ostriches sometimes lie flat on the ground with their long necks stretched out, which helps them blend into the landscape and look less visible to predators.
  • They tend their eggs. Ostriches dig shallow nests in the sand and frequently lower their heads deep into the nest to rotate their eggs. From a distance, this can look like they are burying their heads — and this is probably where the myth got started.

So the idiom is built on a false observation about animal behavior. But here's the beautiful irony: the myth itself perfectly describes the human behavior it has come to represent. The ostrich story, true or not, captures the feeling of foolishly hiding from reality. That's why it stuck around for over 2,000 years.
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This idiom is always negative and critical. When you use it about someone, you are judging them. You are saying they are being:

  • Irresponsible — they are not dealing with something they should deal with.
  • Cowardly — they are afraid to face an uncomfortable truth.
  • Foolish — they believe that ignoring a problem will make it go away.

You would never use this idiom to compliment someone. It carries a strong sense of disapproval.

The idiom can be used to criticize a single person, a company, an organization, or even an entire government. It scales in that way.
How to Use It Grammatically

The idiom is flexible and can be used in many tenses. Notice how the pronoun changes based on who you're talking about:

SituationForm
Talking about yourselfbury my head in the sand
Talking about another personbury his/her/their head in the sand
Talking about a groupbury their heads in the sand

When talking about yourself, you say "bury my head in the sand." When talking about another person, you say "bury his, her, or their head in the sand." When talking about a group, you say "bury their heads in the sand."

The idiom works smoothly across all tenses:

  • Simple present: She buries her head in the sand every time money comes up.
  • Past tense: He buried his head in the sand for years.
  • Present continuous: They are burying their heads in the sand.
  • Present perfect: The company has buried its head in the sand about this issue.
  • Imperative (command): Stop burying your head in the sand!
Examples in Real Life Situations

Here are examples from many different areas of life so you can really feel how it's used:

Personal life:

  • "She knew her marriage was in serious trouble, but she buried her head in the sand and refused to talk about it."
  • "He kept burying his head in the sand about his gambling habit, even as his savings disappeared."

Health:

  • "Don't bury your head in the sand about those chest pains — go see a doctor."
  • "She had been burying her head in the sand about her symptoms for months before she finally went to the hospital."

Finance:

  • "They were deep in debt, but they kept burying their heads in the sand and spending as if nothing was wrong."

Work/Business:

  • "The company buried its head in the sand about the changing market, and eventually went bankrupt."
  • "The manager was burying her head in the sand about the team's poor performance."

Politics and Society:

  • "The government has been burying its head in the sand on climate change for decades."
  • "We can't keep burying our heads in the sand — the city's housing crisis is getting worse every year."
Common Variations of the Idiom

You may also hear slight variations, all with the exact same meaning:

  • "Stick one's head in the sand" — This is just as common as "bury." The two are perfectly interchangeable.
    • "He's been sticking his head in the sand about his health for too long."
  • "Have one's head in the sand" — This version emphasizes the state of being in denial, rather than the action.
    • "The board clearly has its head in the sand on this matter."
Related Idioms (and How They Differ)

These idioms are similar in meaning but have important differences:

"Turn a blind eye"
This means to deliberately ignore something wrong that someone else is doing — often something you have a responsibility to address. It's about ignoring other people's wrongdoing. "Bury one's head in the sand," by contrast, is more about ignoring a problem that threatens you or your own situation.

  • "The supervisor turned a blind eye to the safety violations." (Someone else's wrong behavior)
  • "She buried her head in the sand about her own financial problems." (Her own dangerous situation)

"Sweep something under the rug (or carpet)"
This means to hide a problem or mistake so that others don't find out about it — often there's an element of concealment from others. Burying your head in the sand is more about fooling yourself.

  • "The school tried to sweep the bullying incident under the rug."

"Be in denial"
This is a more psychological phrase meaning to refuse to accept a truth. It's very close in meaning to burying one's head in the sand, and the two are often used in similar situations. "In denial" is slightly more neutral and clinical; "bury one's head in the sand" is more colorful and more strongly critical.

"Ignore the elephant in the room"
This means to avoid talking about an obvious, large problem that everyone can see but no one wants to mention. The main difference is that with the "elephant in the room," everyone knows about the problem. With "burying your head in the sand," the focus is on one person (or group) refusing to see the problem.
Opposite Idioms (What It Means to Do the Opposite)

If someone is not burying their head in the sand, they are doing one of these:

  • "Face the music" — To accept the consequences of a bad situation courageously.
    • "It's time to stop avoiding it and face the music."
  • "Bite the bullet" — To endure a painful or difficult situation bravely.
  • "Face the facts" — To accept reality as it is, even if it's unpleasant.
  • "Confront something head-on" — To deal with a problem directly and without hesitation.
One Very Important Thing to Remember

The most crucial part of this idiom is the idea of choice. The person is not unaware of the problem. They are aware of it — but they choose not to face it. This is what makes it a criticism. You are essentially saying: "You know there's a problem, and you are choosing to pretend it isn't there."

This is very different from saying someone is simply ignorant (unaware). Ignorance means you don't know. Burying your head in the sand means you know — but you refuse to look.
A Quick Summary

To put it all together in one place:

"Bury one's head in the sand" means to intentionally ignore a problem or danger instead of dealing with it, in the false hope that it will go away by itself. It comes from the ancient (but false) myth that ostriches hide their heads in sand when threatened. It is always used critically, never as a compliment. It can describe a person, company, or government. The key idea is that the person knows the problem exists but chooses to avoid it. The opposite of this behavior is to "face the music" or "face the facts" — to look at reality with open eyes and deal with it honestly.
